claims.claim: CCNet trains a per-language 5-gram Kneser-Ney language model on a target high-quality domain such as Wikipedia and uses KenLM to compute paragraph perplexity.
claims.notes: The language model and target domain are language-specific; the score is relative to that reference distribution.

claims.claim: CCNet divides each language's documents into equally sized head, middle and tail groups by perplexity rather than deleting all high-perplexity content.
claims.locator: §3.4 LM filtering and §5.2 Statistics from the language model
claims.notes: The paper explicitly retains tail data because some valid comments and specialized-domain text differ from Wikipedia.

claims.claim: CCNet reports that lower perplexity indicates closer fit to the target domain, but valid specialized forums and spoken-style comments can appear in the high-perplexity tail.
claims.notes: This is the central caveat against interpreting PPL as universal quality.

claims.claim: KenLM's Python Model.score returns a log10 sentence probability and Model.perplexity exponentiates the negative average log10 score using the predicted token count including EOS.
claims.notes: For subword models, pass the same whitespace-separated subword sequence used to train the model.

claims.claim: Perplexity is the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood and depends directly on tokenization, so comparisons require a consistent tokenizer and scoring protocol.
claims.notes: Perplexity is not directly comparable across different tokenizers or incompatible model contexts.
